why: Code-RL also weakens the task-general self-copy pathway, so with the cue at T 1.0 it removes part of the base's 27 cap hits but none of its content errors: a small gain over 410.
A random matched-norm difference does not point along the copy-suppression direction, so the cued base keeps its cap hits and its 410-level accuracy.
A random difference leaves the self-copy pathway intact, so cap hits and mean length stay at the cued base's 3,933 tokens.
Copy suppression arrives early in the dose, so at a = 0.25 part of the cued base's 27 cap hits disappear and mean tokens fall below the base's 3,933 rather than rising toward RL's length.
Min-p 0.1 cuts the low-probability tokens that let T 1.0 escape the copy attractor, so rule-A loops come back from 0 toward the T 0.6 level.
Returning loops run to the cap, raising cap hits well above the 27 at plain T 1.0.
Loops restored by min-p truncation cost the cued base accuracy relative to 410 at untruncated T 1.0.
At T 1.5 with min-p 0.1 enough tail mass survives to escape copying, so loops stay near zero and accuracy stays near the T 1.0 level.
Top-p 0.95 trims part of the escape tail, adding a few loops and costing a few points relative to 410.
RL's self-copy pathway is already weakened, so min-p truncation does not restore loops and RL stays at its 463 level.
The RL change is an input-dependent change to copy circuitry spread over many neurons and heads, so one constant vector per layer closes little of KL(RL||base).
Same reason on RL text: a constant per-layer offset cannot reproduce a context-dependent weakening of copying.
An MLP-only constant offset captures even less of an input-dependent change than the full-layer one.
A cap hit at T 1.0 is the base trapped by its own prefix; a fresh restart escapes it, recovering roughly half of the ~27 cap hits.
